newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI COMPLETES GOLDEN DOUBLE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI COMPLETES GOLDEN DOUBLE.

text.p: Italy's Deborah Compagnoni picked up her second gold medal of the Alpine skiing world championships on Sunday to go where no compatriot, including Alberto Tomba, has gone before.

The double Olympic gold medallist clocked a total time of two minutes 39.19 seconds over the two runs of the giant slalom to win by a healthy margin and become the first Italian to defend an Alpine world title.
Compagnoni also joined Tomba with five career golds, although she has them in more disciplines, and matched his achievement of two titles in one championships.
"There were so many fans here it would have been really awful to let them down," said Compagnoni on a day that saw the crowds turn out in force.
"It was difficult. It may have seemed easy but it was tough," she added of the pressure of skiing at home.
Switzerland's Karin Roten, runner-up in the giant to Compagnoni in the southern Spanish resort of Sierra Nevada in 1996, again finished second in 2:39.99.
She said she had needed a day to recover her concentration for the giant but had been given a big boost by compatriot Bruno Kernen winning the men's downhill on Saturday.
"If he could do it, so could I," she said.

France's Leila Piccard, sister of 1992 Olympic downhill silver medallist Franck who also won a super-G bronze medal in the 1991 championships, finished third after a remarkable comeback from 12th place in the first leg.
Piccard's was France's first medal and made up for the disappointment of men's downhill gold medal favourite Luc Alphand who crashed out of that race.
"I had nothing to lose," Piccard said, adding that her brother had told her to give everything and not to think about what sort of a result she might eventually get.
Franck was in the crowd and seemed more delighted than his sister, putting his sunglasses on to hide the tears.

Compagnoni said her first run, which she could have dominated even more decisively were it not for a major mistake at the finish, proved the key to her victory although she admitted her first gold had made everything easier.
She skied slightly more cautiously on the last run but was second fastest behind Piccard's 1:21.37.
"Winning in Italy is so beautiful. Every medal is special but when you do it here it is perfect," she said.
Compagnoni, who despite her extraordinary success never manages to shake off the comparisons with Tomba in Italy, said she hoped her golds would help him next week.

"I hope that he is relaxed and goes well. He's more experienced than me and he won the last slalom so I hope he does well," she said of the slalom and giant champion who succesfully defended his 1988 Olympic giant title in 1992.
Piccard's time dashed the hopes of Austrian veteran Anita Wachter, who was fourth as she had been last year and as she was at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics.
"I was the fastest at the top but then I didn't attack at the bottom on the flat. I knew that it wouldn't be enough for a medal when I got to the finish," Wachter said sadly.
"Compagnoni is not unbeatable. "The main problem is that she has so much confidence."

Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg, who won two golds in Sierra Nevada, continued her barren streak with sixth place. The overall World Cup leader had looked strong on the second run but lost a ski pole one gate before the finish.
Martina Ertl, the 1996 bronze medallist, finished a distant 12th but was pleased with her performance.
She had defied specialists who gave her no chance of competing in the championships because of a knee injury sustained in Italy in January. She competed with a special brace.
